strengths: Addresses a novel and practically relevant problem: reconstructing sharp animatable 3D Gaussian human avatars from motion-blurred multi-view video, which has not been previously tackled to my knowledge.

The proposed 3D-aware blur formation model is a sensible extension of physics-based 2D blur formulation (averaging virtual sharp images) into the SMPL-driven Gaussian avatar setting, allowing joint optimization of sub-frame motion and canonical avatar appearance.

The sub-frame motion model combining B-spline interpolation of pose with a non-rigid displacement network is a reasonable way to balance smooth global motion trajectories with higher-frequency pose variation, and the inter-frame regularization loss addressing directional ambiguity (Fig. 1c, Fig. 7) is a nice, well-motivated design choice with clear empirical justification.

The paper contributes two new benchmark datasets (a ZJU-MoCap-based synthetic set and a real 360-degree hybrid-exposure captured dataset) which could be a useful resource for future work in this underexplored task, given the current lack of benchmarks.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided (pose interpolation vs. per-frame, non-rigid displacement, LBS/shape optimization, control knot number, virtual image count, blur magnitude Kblur, and regularization loss), which support the design choices with quantitative and qualitative evidence.
Quantitative results consistently show improvement over the compared 3DGS-avatar + 2D-deblurring baselines across both synthetic and real datasets, across multiple blur magnitudes.
weaknesses: Baselines are limited to combinations of existing 2D video deblurring networks with GauHuman; no comparison to any dedicated 3D-aware deblurring approach for dynamic scenes (e.g. DyBluRF, BAD-Gaussians/BAD-NeRF adapted or extended) is attempted, even though such comparisons might be feasible with modification, leaving unclear how much of the gain is due to the human-specific 3D-aware formulation versus simply having any 3D-consistent bundle-adjustment-like framework.

Improvements over the two-stage 2D-deblur+GauHuman baselines are numerically modest in absolute PSNR/SSIM terms in some settings despite being described as 'significant' (e.g., Table 3 real data: 27.01 vs 25.6 PSNR, ~0.02 SSIM gain over best baseline), and the paper does not report any statistical variance, error bars, or per-scene breakdown to assess robustness of the reported gains, especially given only 6 synthetic subjects and 8 real scenes.

The real dataset construction uses a fixed, single blur/sharp exposure ratio (16x) and a small number of scenes (8) with limited motion diversity/description, which constrains how well the benchmark generalizes to broader blur conditions or more complex human motions (e.g. fast athletic movement, occlusion, multiple people).

The acknowledged limitation regarding blending between foreground/background during blur (Fig. 8) and reliance on pre-computed hard masks is a nontrivial modeling gap that could materially affect quality, particularly for real captures with high-contrast backgrounds, yet no quantitative analysis of its severity is given.

The paper is a fairly direct, if well-executed, combination of existing techniques (BAD-NeRF/BAD-Gaussians-style blur formation, B-spline pose interpolation as in USB-NeRF, GauHuman-style avatar model) applied to a new but incrementally different setting; the core technical novelty is primarily the domain adaptation rather than a fundamentally new formulation, which should be weighed against the contribution.

There are noticeable presentation issues, including a large duplicated paragraph in Section 2.1 (the same 'In recent years, the deblurring paradigm...' text appears twice, once at the end of 2.1 and once continuing to page 3), which suggests the manuscript was not carefully proofread before submission.

Table 6 results show that even without the Lreg regularization, the middle-timestep performance is essentially the same or occasionally better (e.g., PSNR 25.567 vs 25.546 for Kblur=5), meaning the primary benefit of Lreg is confined to non-middle timesteps, which are not directly assessable on the real dataset and only weakly justified as important to the main deblurring task (i.e. producing correct video frames vs. simply correct middle-frame appearance).

strengths: Addresses a novel and practically relevant problem: reconstructing sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian human avatars directly from motion-blurred multi-view video, which is the first work in this specific niche to the best of the reviewer's knowledge.

Principled 3D-aware blur formation model that extends the standard 2D blur integral to the SMPL/3DGS animatable avatar setting, decomposing the problem into sub-frame motion estimation and canonical avatar reconstruction in a physically motivated way.

The sub-frame motion model (B-spline pose interpolation + CNN-based pose deformation + inter-frame geodesic regularization) is a reasonable and well-justified design to resolve the motion ambiguity illustrated in Fig. 1, and ablations (Tabs. 3-4, Figs. 7-8) support each component's contribution.

Solid benchmark contribution: a synthetic ZJU-MoCap-derived blur dataset plus a custom 360-degree hybrid-exposure real camera system providing paired blurry/sharp multi-view captures, which could be useful to the community if released.

Extensive robustness studies across blur magnitude, number of training views, mask estimation quality, SMPL initialization perturbation, control-knot count, and virtual frame number, plus a smartphone demo, giving a fairly thorough picture of the method's behavior under varied conditions.
Clear ablations isolating the value of pose interpolation, non-rigid pose deformation, LBS refinement, and shape optimization, with both quantitative and qualitative support.
weaknesses: Comparisons are limited to a single avatar backbone (GauHuman) combined with generic 2D video deblurring methods; no comparison against blur-aware NeRF/3DGS methods for dynamic scenes that are discussed in related work (e.g., DyBluRF, BAD-Gaussians/BAD-NeRF-style approaches, BAD-GS), even in adapted form, leaving open whether the proposed 3D-aware approach clearly surpasses existing blur-aware dynamic-scene reconstruction techniques rather than only naive 2D-deblur-then-fit pipelines.

Improvements on the real dataset are noticeably smaller than on synthetic data (PSNR ~27.0 vs ~25.5-25.6 for baselines, a much narrower gap than on synthetic data), and the real dataset itself is small (8 scenes, 4 blur views), raising questions about the statistical robustness and generalization of the reported gains.

The paper acknowledges but does not address the fact that averaging is performed in non-linear sRGB space rather than linear radiance space, which is the physically correct location for blur integration; this could materially affect the accuracy of the blur formation model on real data and is left entirely as future work rather than analyzed empirically.

Generality across avatar architectures is unverified since only GauHuman is used as backbone; it is unclear whether the proposed motion/blur modeling transfers to other prominent Gaussian avatar frameworks (3DGS-Avatar, GaussianAvatar, Animatable Gaussians) cited in the introduction.

No runtime/complexity comparison is provided; the joint optimization of sub-frame SMPL motion, pose deformation CNN, LBS offset CNN, and canonical 3DGS likely incurs substantially higher training cost than baselines, which is not quantified despite being relevant for practical adoption.

Reliance on SMPL fundamentally limits handling of loose garments/handheld objects, as acknowledged, and this limitation is not empirically bounded (e.g., no experiment quantifying failure severity on such subjects) beyond a qualitative remark.

strengths: Novel problem formulation: to the best of the reported related work, this is the first paper to directly address reconstruction of sharp, animatable 3D Gaussian human avatars from motion-blurred multi-view video, rather than treating deblurring and avatar reconstruction as separate stages.

The 3D-aware blur formation model is a sensible and well-motivated extension of the classical 2D blur-as-temporal-averaging formulation to the SMPL/3DGS avatar setting, explicitly connecting sub-frame SMPL motion to the rendered blurry observation.

The proposed 3D human motion model (B-spline sub-frame pose interpolation + CNN-based non-rigid pose displacement + LBS offset refinement + shape refinement) is a reasonably complete treatment of the sources of ambiguity in blur-induced pose recovery, and each component is individually ablated with both quantitative (Tab. 3) and qualitative (Fig. 7) evidence.

The inter-frame motion regularization loss is a clever, well-justified addition targeting a specific failure mode (directional ambiguity at non-midpoint timesteps), and the paper provides convincing ablation evidence (Tab. 4, Fig. 8) that it specifically improves non-middle timestep quality without hurting the midpoint quality.

Introduction of a new real-world benchmark using a custom 360-degree hybrid-exposure camera rig (synchronized blurry + sharp views) fills a genuine gap, since no other blur-aware avatar benchmark currently exists; this could be a valuable community resource if released as promised.

Extensive robustness studies are provided: perturbed SMPL initialization, varying blur magnitude, varying number of training views, different mask estimators, and a qualitative real-world smartphone (iPhone 16 Pro) demo, which together support the claim of practical robustness beyond the curated benchmarks.

The method consistently and non-trivially outperforms both a naive blurry-input baseline and several strong two-stage (2D deblur + GauHuman) baselines on both synthetic and real datasets across PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS.
weaknesses: Comparisons are restricted to a single avatar backbone (GauHuman) combined with various 2D deblurring front-ends; no comparison to other modern avatar frameworks (e.g., 3DGS-Avatar, GaussianAvatar, Animatable Gaussians) or to dedicated 3D/NeRF-based deblurring approaches (e.g., BAD-Gaussians, DyBluRF, BARD-GS) adapted to the avatar setting, which limits confidence that gains are specific to the proposed formulation rather than to backbone choice.

Novel-pose animation results (Fig. 13) are only qualitative; no quantitative metric is reported for this important use case of animatable avatars, weakening the evidence for the 'animatable' claim beyond training-time viewpoints.

The acknowledged limitation of averaging non-linear sRGB values instead of linear radiance is a non-trivial physical inaccuracy in the core blur formation model, yet its actual quantitative impact is not measured or ablated, leaving open how much this affects the reported results.

Real-world dataset has a modest scale (8 scenes, 4 blurry views), which constrains how strongly generalization claims to diverse real-world capture conditions can be supported by the presented evidence.

The iPhone 16 Pro demo, the paper's main evidence for monocular/consumer-camera applicability, is qualitative only with no quantitative ground truth comparison, so robustness claims for the most practically relevant capture scenario remain anecdotal.

Computational cost/training time of the joint optimization (multiple CNNs, B-spline interpolation, per-sub-frame rendering) is not reported, making it hard to assess practicality relative to baselines.

The method inherits SMPL's inability to model loose garments or handheld objects, which is acknowledged but leaves a fairly common failure case unaddressed, potentially limiting real-world applicability.
